title: Magnitude 7.0 Earthquake in Tibet Kills 16, Injures 65 as Rescue Expands
excerpt: The late-night quake in Baqen County collapsed at least 339 homes and displaced more than 12,000 people, with rescuers working at extreme altitude in subfreezing conditions.
body:
• A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck Baqen County in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at 10:33 p.m. local time on Thursday, killing at least 16 people and injuring 65, with 11 in serious condition.
  • At least 339 homes collapsed and more than 12,000 residents were evacuated, as over 1,600 rescuers deployed to a high-altitude epicentre above 4,800 metres.
  • President Xi Jinping ordered all-out search and rescue efforts; 1,000 prefabricated housing units, thousands of tents and folding beds were dispatched as subfreezing temperatures and snow approached.
  • Officials cautioned the toll is provisional: injury counts rose from 32 to 65 through Friday morning as communications were restored, and damage surveys are incomplete.

At least 16 people were killed and 65 injured after a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck northern Tibet late on Thursday, flattening hundreds of homes and forcing more than 12,000 residents from their houses. The quake hit Baqen County in Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. local time, when many residents were indoors, according to reports carried by The Sun and The American Quorum, both citing Chinese state media and local authorities. Eleven of the injured were described as being in serious condition.

The death toll held at 16 across the latest accounts, while the injury count rose through Friday morning — from an initial 32 in Xinhua's reporting to 46, then 54, and then 65 in a later local update cited by Reuters. Officials and reporters covering the response cautioned that the figures are provisional, with access and communications disrupted in parts of the county.

Damage and evacuation

The Associated Press reported at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds collapsed; Xinhua put homes collapsed or damaged at more than 330. More than 12,000 residents were evacuated. The U.S. Geological Survey placed the epicentre about 119 miles (roughly 183-191 km) east-northeast of Nagqu, at a depth of about 11 miles (18 km), in a sparsely populated, mountainous region. China's seismic network estimated a shallower depth of about 10 km. CCTV described it as the biggest earthquake in the region in five years.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2113518281495544289

At least seven aftershocks between magnitude 4.3 and 5.2 followed the main shock in early counts, with China's network later recording hundreds of smaller aftershocks. Rockfalls blocked part of National Highway 317, rail services through the area were halted as a precaution, and some quake-hit areas reported power and telecom outages.

"All-out efforts must be made to search for and rescue people trapped by the earthquake."

— Xi Jinping, President of China, via state media

Rescue at extreme altitude

More than 1,600 local personnel, including police and firefighters, moved toward the epicentral area, which sits at an average elevation above 4,800 metres (about 15,700 feet), where thin air slows strenuous work. Authorities dispatched 1,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,000 tents and folding beds, quilts, stoves, flashlights and winter clothing. Rescued residents were taken to sports fields and given makeshift beds and blankets.

President Xi Jinping ordered a mass rescue operation and stressed that the affected area is at high altitude with cold temperatures, urging rescuers to minimise casualties. Forecasters expected lows near minus 9 degrees Celsius over the following three days, with intermittent snow in townships near the epicentre, making shelter and heating as urgent as the search itself.

A seismically exposed plateau

The Tibetan Plateau sits on the collision zone between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates, which produces frequent strong earthquakes. A magnitude 7.1 quake in the Shigatse region in a previous disaster killed more than 125 people and damaged buildings across parts of Tibet, with tremors felt in Nepal and India. Thursday's quake was shallower and in a more remote county, which limited the population near the epicentre but still destroyed hundreds of rural homes.

Damage assessments remain incomplete. The priorities through the weekend are locating survivors, treating the seriously injured, keeping displaced residents warm and reopening roads into remote villages. The confirmed toll should be expected to change as survey teams reach settlements cut off by rockfalls and outages.
